Turning to start up the hunt for a passable nap spot, something caught his eye. He stopped. Turned back slowly, not sure yet what he'd seen, just the peripheral awareness of something that didn't fit — a quality of light, a stillness that struck differently somehow. One of the classrooms off the main hallway. He looked at it for a moment from the corridor. A single desk sat in the middle of the floor. The rest of the room was the same wreckage as everywhere else — waterlogged, debris- strewn, the detritus of the night settling wherever gravity had put it. But the desk was clear. Centred. The streetlight came through the window at an angle that caught it directly, the amber glow pooling across the surface, making it look almost like an altar. He drifted forward, feet whispering through the remaining puddles that sat still and undisturbed on the tile. In the center of the desk sat his robe. Clean. Dry. The leather smooth and unmarked, the canvas underlayer pressed flat, the whole thing arranged with intent that bordered on domestic care. His mask rested on top, face up, the white of it catching the streetlight from the window. His phone and knife bordering it to either side. All of it exactly as it had been before the night started. His entire identity, returned to him like a present. A prize for surviving. Maybe a punishment for not dying. Danny stood in front of the desk and dripped quietly onto the floor. He looked at his things for a long moment without touching them, the clear message from them gently circling his mind. Time’s up. Get back to work. That was what this was. Not a gift — it had never been a gift; he understood that now with a clarity that the night had earned him the hard way. A summons. The gear cleaned and folded and waiting, because tools got maintained between uses, because that was what you did with something you intended to keep using. The cleaning wasn't kindness. It was just upkeep. He'd known, in the abstract, that this was how it worked. He'd always known. The killers weren't here because She loved them — they were here because She needed them, and need was a transactional thing. He'd told himself the autonomy he'd carved out was real, that the space between the trials was his, that the arrangement was something he'd chosen to participate in rather than something he'd been slotted into. The water in the schoolyard said otherwise. She had turned Her domain into a trap and put him in it with the survivors without warning or protection, and when it stopped serving Her purposes, She had simply — withdrawn. Left him to whatever came next. The gear on the desk was not an apology. It was a reminder of what he was for, laid out under a streetlight like a receipt. He knew better than to disobey. He had seen what Her displeasure looked like up close tonight, felt it in the current that had no interest in which side of the trial he was supposed to be on. If She decided he wasn't worth the trouble of maintaining, that was simply what would happen. They were all tools. Every one of them. Expected to be grateful She'd found a use for them at all. He picked up the robe. The leather was dry. Clean. Lighter than it had been in the hallway, obviously — waterlogged was a different animal entirely — but he suspected She had given back his strength before withdrawing as well. He stood with it in his hands for a moment, feeling the familiar weight of it. Eventually, with hands that trembled more than he wanted to admit, he dressed. Layer by layer, the same way it came off — in reverse, without ceremony, the buckles finding their positions with the muscle memory of a hundred trials. The cowl. The gloves. The whole assembled architecture of the thing, rebuilt around him in the amber light of an empty classroom while water dripped quietly in the hallway behind him. He picked up the knife last. Ran his thumb along the worn edge of the handle, the familiar curves of it sitting in his palm exactly as they always had. He waited for the thing that usually came with it — the sharpening of attention, the quiet pleasure of holding something he was good at using. The sense of himself clicking back into place. It didn't come. He closed his hand around the handle anyway and slid it home. He knew how the next trial would go. He'd stalk, and he'd slash, and he'd play the game the way he'd always played it, because that’s what was expected of him and he knew better than to refuse. He'd find the rhythm of it again eventually. Maybe even the fun. The Fog had a way of smoothing things over, filing the edges down, making the distances between things feel longer than they were. But for a select few, he would hold back. Not many. Just a handful. Just enough to make a difference that nobody would be able to measure or name — a fraction of a second's hesitation, a hook instead of a blade, a hatch left open for no particular reason. Not mercy. He wasn't prepared to call it that. Just a fraction. Just enough. The smallest seeds of doubt, buried deep in the Fog.
